write.desc: Infinite series of real numbers defined as limits of their partial sums, with the convergence tests proved as theorems from sequence results, absolute versus conditional convergence, rearrangements and products; the points belong together because each one turns a question about a series into a question about the sequence of its partial sums.

points.name: A series is the limit of its partial sums
points.what: Define the partial sums S_n of a series, what it means for the series to converge to a sum or diverge (including diverging to plus or minus infinity), and explain why the sum is a limit of a sequence, not an infinite addition.
outside: epsilon-N definition of the limit of a sequence
divergence of a sequence to infinity

points.name: Algebra of series and tails
points.what: Prove that convergent series can be added and multiplied by constants term by term, that changing or deleting finitely many terms does not affect convergence, and that the tails of a convergent series tend to 0.
outside: limit laws for sequences (sum and constant multiple)

points.name: Geometric series
points.what: Compute the partial sums of the geometric series in closed form and prove it converges to a/(1-r) exactly when |r| < 1, so it can serve as the benchmark for later comparisons.
outside: the limit of r^n for |r| < 1 and its divergence for |r| >= 1

points.name: Telescoping series
points.what: Recognise series whose terms are differences b_n - b_(n+1), show their partial sums collapse to b_1 - b_(n+1), and evaluate sums such as the sum of 1/(n(n+1)).
outside: limit laws for sequences (sum and constant multiple)

points.name: The term test and the harmonic series
points.what: Prove that if a series converges then its terms tend to 0, use the contrapositive to show divergence, and prove by grouping terms that the harmonic series diverges, so the converse of the term test is false.
outside: contrapositive of an implication
limit laws for sequences (sum and constant multiple)

points.name: Cauchy criterion for series
points.what: State and prove that a series converges if and only if for every epsilon > 0 the blocks of terms a_(m+1) + ... + a_n are smaller than epsilon for all large n > m, and use it to show convergence without knowing the sum.
outside: Cauchy criterion for sequences (a sequence of reals converges iff it is Cauchy)

points.name: Series with nonnegative terms
points.what: Prove that a series of nonnegative terms converges if and only if its partial sums are bounded, because its partial sums are increasing, and see why such a series either converges or diverges to infinity.
outside: monotone convergence theorem for sequences

points.name: Comparison test
points.what: Prove that if 0 <= a_n <= b_n eventually then convergence of the sum of b_n gives convergence of the sum of a_n and divergence of the sum of a_n gives divergence of the sum of b_n, and use geometric and harmonic series as comparison series.

points.name: Limit comparison test
points.what: Prove that if a_n, b_n > 0 and a_n/b_n tends to a finite positive limit then the two series converge or diverge together, and use it to handle series that are dominated by their leading term, such as rational functions of n.
outside: order limit theorem for sequences (a convergent sequence with limit L > 0 is eventually between L/2 and 2L)

points.name: Cauchy condensation test
points.what: Prove that for a decreasing sequence of nonnegative terms the sum of a_n converges if and only if the sum of 2^k a_(2^k) converges, by bounding partial sums of one series by partial sums of the other.

points.name: p-series
points.what: Use the condensation test and the geometric series to prove that the sum of 1/n^p converges exactly when p > 1, and add p-series to the stock of comparison series (including series like the sum of 1/(n (log n)^p)).

points.name: Alternating series (Leibniz) test
points.what: Prove that if a_n decreases to 0 then the sum of (-1)^(n+1) a_n converges, by showing the even and odd partial sums are monotone and squeeze together, and that the error after n terms is at most a_(n+1).
outside: monotone convergence theorem for sequences
a sequence converges if its even-indexed and odd-indexed subsequences converge to the same limit

points.name: Absolute and conditional convergence
points.what: Define absolute and conditional convergence, prove from the Cauchy criterion and the triangle inequality that absolute convergence implies convergence, and use the alternating harmonic series to show the converse fails.
outside: triangle inequality for absolute value

points.name: Ratio test
points.what: Prove by comparison with a geometric series that the series converges absolutely if limsup |a_(n+1)/a_n| < 1 and diverges if |a_(n+1)/a_n| >= 1 eventually, and show with p-series that the test says nothing when the ratio tends to 1.
outside: limit superior and limit inferior of a sequence

points.name: Root test with limsup
points.what: Prove that the series converges absolutely if limsup |a_n|^(1/n) < 1 and diverges if it is greater than 1, explain why limsup rather than lim makes the test always applicable, and know that the root test decides every case the ratio test decides.
outside: limit superior and limit inferior of a sequence
the limit of n^(1/n) is 1

points.name: Rearranging absolutely convergent series
points.what: Define a rearrangement as reordering the terms by a bijection of the natural numbers and prove that every rearrangement of an absolutely convergent series converges to the same sum.
outside: bijections of the natural numbers
epsilon-N definition of the limit of a sequence

points.name: Riemann rearrangement theorem
points.what: Prove that for a conditionally convergent series the positive and negative parts both diverge, and use this to rearrange it to converge to any chosen real number or to diverge, showing why conditional convergence depends on the order of the terms.
outside: bijections of the natural numbers

points.name: Products of series (Cauchy product)
points.what: Define the Cauchy product of two series, prove that if both converge absolutely the product converges absolutely to the product of the sums, state Mertens' theorem (one absolutely convergent factor suffices), and see an example of two convergent series whose Cauchy product diverges.

points.name: Decimal expansions as series
points.what: Interpret an infinite decimal as a series of digits times powers of 10, prove that it always converges by comparison with a geometric series, show every real number in [0,1) has a decimal expansion, and explain why 0.999... = 1.
outside: Archimedean property and the floor (integer part) of a real number
supremum and the completeness axiom

points.name: Choosing and justifying a convergence test
points.what: Given a series, decide which test settles it (term test, comparison or limit comparison with geometric or p-series, condensation, ratio, root, alternating series test) and write a complete justification that checks every hypothesis of the test used.

where.title: Stephen Abbott, Understanding Analysis (2nd ed.)
where.detail: Section 2.1 (rearrangements of the alternating harmonic series), 2.4 (series and the Cauchy condensation test), 2.7 (properties of infinite series), 2.8 (double summations and products of series)

where.title: Robert G. Bartle and Donald R. Sherbert, Introduction to Real Analysis (4th ed.)
where.detail: Section 3.7 (introduction to infinite series) and Chapter 9 (absolute convergence, tests for absolute convergence, tests for nonabsolute convergence)

where.title: Walter Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis (3rd ed.)
